author: vdmkenny
body:
167 tests. Adds `karst-mix::exposure` and `docs/18-documented-attacks.md`.

Every other document here reasons about adversaries in the abstract. This audits KARST against three deanonymisations that happened to real people. **Two would work against it, and one failure is new.**

## BKA against Boystown, 2019 to 2021

Four stages: run many Tor nodes, correlate timing, discover the guard, then a Frankfurt court order to Telefónica naming the o2 subscriber.

| Stage | KARST |
|---|---|
| Run many nodes | **Fails.** L16 confirmed insufficient, L5 admission unbuilt |
| Timing correlation | **Holds.** The thing it spent most effort on |
| Guard discovery | **Holds.** Socially introduced entry; an attacker cannot volunteer |
| ISP names the subscriber | **Fails, and worse than Tor** |

## The new finding: constant-rate emission is an ISP signature

The BKA case *ended* at the access provider, and that stage has never been examined here.

L3 hides what the bytes are. It does not hide what shape they arrive in, and L4 mandates a shape nothing else on a residential line produces.

| Profile | Rate variability |
|---|---|
| Ordinary browsing and streaming | > 0.8 |
| **L4 constant-rate emission** | **0.00** |

`karst-mix::exposure` measures a classifier separating them at **above 99% accuracy using a byte counter** — no payload inspection, no protocol fingerprinting, no ML. Every access provider already runs that measurement for billing.

The anonymity set is not everyone on the network, it is everyone *on that ISP* emitting at a constant rate. Early in deployment that is a workable shortlist. **The mechanism that provides anonymity at scale removes it when few people are using it.** Cost 6.13a, filed rather than fixed.

## CMU/CERT relay-early, 2014

A Sybil fleet plus a **tagging attack**: modify protocol headers so a colluding relay recognises traffic that passed a confederate.

`karst-mix::packet` is documented as "Sphinx-shaped but not Sphinx", with a BLAKE3 keystream and **no per-hop MAC**, so it has none of Sphinx's tagging resistance. **This attack works today.** #1 moves from a correctness item to a known-exploited class.

## FBI NIT against Playpen, 2015

Half the playbook does not apply: there is no unique host to seize and operate.

The other half is the clearest practical argument for L10's austerity. No scripting, deny-by-default sandbox, no ambient network access from content, and a format small enough that the attack surface is a typed node decoder rather than a browser with a JIT. Reduced, not removed, and only for content not reached through a gateway.

## One hazard the Ricochet detail exposes

The victim was running a version lacking current guard protections. Tor had shipped the defence; it was not on that endpoint. **KARST has no update mechanism and no way for a user to learn their client is missing a defence.** A defence that exists and is not running is worth nothing.

## The pattern

KARST wins where it spent effort and loses where it assumed. The timing defence was simulated repeatedly and holds. The packet format was labelled proof-of-concept and never revisited. The ISP relationship was never examined at all, and it is where the only real-world case here actually ended.

author: sumit-m
body:
## Problem

`ensure_skill_symlinks` is a no-op on non-Unix. The canonical skill is written to
`.agents/skills/buzz-cli/SKILL.md`, but nothing links to it, so on Windows the
harness skill directories are never created:

```
$ ls ~/.buzz-dev/.agents/skills/buzz-cli/SKILL.md
SKILL.md                                  <- written
$ ls ~/.buzz-dev/.claude/skills
No such file or directory                 <- never created
$ ls ~/.buzz-dev/.goose/skills
No such file or directory
```

`nest_skill.md` is the document that teaches an agent the CLI it uses to publish
every reply. On Windows no agent has ever loaded it.

## Fix

`ensure_skill_symlinks` becomes platform-neutral and uses `create_dir_link`,
which tries `symlink_dir` and falls back to a junction — neither Developer Mode
nor elevation required. A new `skill_link_target` picks the target form:
relative on Unix, absolute on Windows, because junctions store only absolute
targets.

Unix behaviour is unchanged by construction — `create_dir_link` on Unix is the
same `std::os::unix::fs::symlink` the previous code called, and the relative
target string is pinned by a test.

### A second hole in the same area

`refresh_skill_md_if_stale` removes the old real `.claude/skills/buzz-cli`
directory on *every* platform but re-created the link only under `#[cfg(unix)]`.
On Windows a `NEST_SKILL_VERSION` bump would have deleted the directory and left
nothing behind. Made platform-neutral in the same commit.

## Tests

The three skill-link tests were `#[cfg(unix)]`, so the platform that was broken
had no coverage. They now run everywhere:

- relative-target assertion stays Unix-only; a new test asserts the absolute
  target on Windows
- the dangling-link test creates its link and *then* deletes the target — a
  junction cannot be created against a target that does not exist

Also removes three dead-code warnings that only appeared on Windows
(`known_skill_dirs` import and function, `runtime_metadata::skill_dir`).

## Notes for review

**Overlap with #3547.** `create_dir_link` and `remove_dir_link` are identical to
the versions in that PR, which has not merged. They are carried here so this
branch compiles standalone. Happy to rebase onto whichever lands first.

**Reproducing on Windows needs the dev-tooling PRs.** `just dev` cannot run off
`main` on Windows — the Tauri `beforeDevCommand` is `exec ./node_modules/.bin/vite`
and cmd.exe has no `exec` (#3534). Verification here ran on `main` plus #3534,
#3546, #3545 and #3540, with this commit's diff confirmed untouched by that
merge. The fix itself depends on none of them.

## Verification

On Windows 11, Developer Mode off, non-elevated process:

- deleted all three existing links, booted, all three came back as
  `LinkType=Junction` resolving to `.agents/skills/buzz-cli/SKILL.md`
- an agent asked to list its skills named `buzz-cli`; `~/.claude/skills` is empty
  on that box, so the nest link is the only possible source
- desktop lib suite: 1946 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure

body:
## What was wrong

Tick a filter value under a layer that is **not switched on yet**, then switch that layer on: the map draws every record in the file while the counter beside it reports the filtered number.

Measured on production (`dbfc32c`), racial covenants, one city ticked before the layer was switched on:

| | sidebar counter | features actually handed to the map |
|---|---|---|
| after switching the layer on | `4` | **2567** |
| after clicking Clear filters | `2567` | 2567 |

`loadLayer()` handed `addLayer()` the whole layer, and `setFilter()` -> `refresh()` returns early while the source does not exist yet, so a filter ticked before the data arrived was stored and never drawn. Every redraw *after* that point used `filteredFeatures()`, which is why the bug only ever showed on a layer's first paint.

This is what "clear filters does nothing" was: with the map never filtered in the first place, clearing changed the counter and left the canvas exactly as it was.

## The fix

One line — the first paint takes the filtered set, the same one every later redraw takes.

## Verified

Against a local build of this branch, driven in a real browser:

- filter-before-switch-on: counter `4`, drawn **4** (was 2567); clearing restores both to 2567
- control, the other order (switch on, then filter): unchanged, `1` and `1`
- full clear-filters sweep over all five filterable layers — 287(g), ALPR, redlining, data centres, covenants — every one narrows and restores, no boxes left ticked
- WebKit re-run of the clear-filters path: checkboxes, counts, reach slider and search box all reset, no console errors

## Not in this PR

The ALPR corridor layer advertises a **Road type** filter that renders nothing — the corridor rework dropped `roadClass` from the emitted data, so `distinctValues` finds none. Either the ingest should carry it again or the registry entry should go; flagging it rather than folding it in here.

**Meu erro foi o glob:** varri `**/Routes/*.php` com `R` maiúsculo; o KB usa `Http/routes.php` minúsculo, e o padrão nunca casou. Classe **LC-08** — afirmar a partir da fonte errada. Quem pegou foi [W], relendo o que a sessão anterior tinha registrado.

**A conclusão sobrevive, por outra razão.** As telas não são a mesma:

| | `/kb/graph` | `/ads/admin/graph` |
|---|---|---|
| render | `kb/Graph` por **closure, sem props** | `ads/Admin/Graph` via `GraphController` |
| dado | `/kb/graph/data` → `{nodes:[],edges:[],kpis:null}` — o próprio teste diz *"A TELA É FACHADA"* | 5 fontes reais |

Matar a do ADS teria trocado a tela **com dado** pela **fachada**. Fica registrado que a conclusão sobreviveu por sorte; a medição que a sustentava, não.

## 2. Migration — remove 10 permissions Spatie órfãs

Decisão [W] nomeou as 6 `ads.admin.skills.*`. As outras 4 (`ads.access`, `ads.decisoes.review|approve`, `ads.policy.manage`) seguem pela **mesma razão**: a tela que cada uma protegia caiu no #5135, e o `DataController` que as declarava na tela de Roles já não existe — ninguém consegue mais marcá-las.

**Ordem importa:** concessões (`role_has_permissions`/`model_has_permissions`) **antes** da permission — a ADR 0363 §3 registra que elas referenciam por **id de linha**. O `down()` recria as permissions mas **não** as concessões (os ids morreram com as linhas): reversibilidade honesta, não completa.

## 3. Baselines — 2 de 3

- `casos-coverage`: as 14 telas mortas saem, as 5 vivas ficam;
- `module-grades`: entrada `ADS` removida — para de reportar `⚠️ removed` em todo PR, o vermelho crônico que o próprio comentário do baseline critica.

## 4. `eslint-baseline` NÃO tocado, de propósito

Editei e **reverti**: o `_meta.total_violations` (2664) já estava dessincronizado da soma real (2575) **antes** de mim. Mexer à mão num baseline com meta fora de sincronia é inventar número — a limpeza dessas 18 entradas tem que vir do gerador. Declarado em vez de silenciado.

## O que este PR NÃO toca

- `ads_module` em `package_details` — ato de superadmin, não de refactor (ADR 0363 §4);
- URLs e nomes de rota `ads.admin.*` sobreviventes — congelados pela **[ADR 0087](memory/decisions/0087-drift-resolution-sem-mover-url.md)**, que segue `aceito`/`ativo` e **não foi superada**: ela proíbe *mover* URL ao resolver drift, não proíbe remover tela.

## Summary

- Snapshot tensor arguments declared in each Helion kernel's `mutates_args` metadata.
- Restore those arguments before every warmup and measured launch so each repetition sees the same inputs.
- Exclude reset and L2-cache-clear setup from event timings, and subtract the equivalent setup graph from CUDA-graph timings.

## Dependency

This PR is stacked on #48968. The reset-specific change is commit `a25ead35fe`; the branch will be rebased onto `main` after #48968 merges. Do not merge this PR before #48968.

## Duplicate check

Searched open `vllm-project/vllm` PRs for `Helion benchmark reset input`, `benchmark_helion_kernels mutated inputs`, `CUDA graph input reset benchmark`, and `Helion input mutation benchmark`. No PR addressing this change was found.

## Performance

Measured on GB200 with the CUDA baseline and CUDA graphs. Each result is the median of five trial means, with reset/no-reset and CUDA/Helion execution order alternated between trials. Both variants use the same timing implementation; the no-reset control passes a no-op callback.

Representative shapes use `num_tokens=128` and `group_size=128`; hidden size is 4096 for per-token quant and RMSNorm, and intermediate size is 6144 for SiLU.

| Kernel | CUDA, no reset (ms) | CUDA, reset (ms) | Helion, no reset (ms) | Helion, reset (ms) | Speedup, no reset | Speedup, reset | Delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `per_token_group_fp8_quant` | 0.003845 | 0.003886 | 0.002285 | 0.002305 | 1.683x | 1.686x | +0.2% |
| `silu_and_mul_per_block_quant` | 0.006130 | 0.006078 | 0.002813 | 0.002702 | 2.179x | 2.249x | +3.2% |
| `rms_norm_per_block_quant` | 0.006803 | 0.006998 | 0.003712 | 0.003634 | 1.833x | 1.926x | +5.1% |

The output-only per-token kernel is effectively unchanged. RMSNorm changes because its residual is read and updated in place: without reset, repetitions accumulate the residual and benchmark progressively different inputs. The reset version consistently benchmarks the original input state. Differences for these microsecond-scale kernels also include normal run-to-run measurement variance.

## Testing

- `uv run --python /home/shangdiy/.conda/envs/vllm-release/bin/python --no-project python -m pytest tests/kernels/helion/test_benchmark_script.py -q`: 5 passed.
- `uvx ruff@0.14.0 check scripts/benchmark_helion_kernels.py tests/kernels/helion/test_benchmark_script.py`: passed.
- `uvx ruff@0.14.0 format --check scripts/benchmark_helion_kernels.py tests/kernels/helion/test_benchmark_script.py`: passed.
- All commit-time pre-commit hooks passed, including ruff, mypy, typos, SPDX, sign-off, and repository policy hooks.
- GB200 RMSNorm integration with both event and CUDA-graph timing verified that Helion and CUDA leave the residual at exactly one fused-add update after repeated benchmarking; all measured latencies were positive.

Model evaluation is not applicable because this changes a standalone developer benchmark and does not affect serving or model outputs.

author: judefleming134
body:
Ferrari pass on the cron that must never be left broken. Two things — one faster, one safer.

## Faster

`sendReviewReminders` was awaited **first, in series**, ahead of everything else. It touches only `ra_customers` and `businesses`; every task after it touches `ge_*` and `strategy_bookings`:

```
sendReviewReminders  →  businesses, ra_customers
the ge_ chain        →  ge_activities, ge_meetings, ge_messages,
                        ge_prospects, ge_research, ge_team_members,
                        strategy_bookings
```

Fully disjoint. There's nothing to race, and no reason for several outbound reminder emails — a network round trip each — to sit on the critical path of a **60-second budget that also has to fit an AI call for the brief**.

It now starts immediately and is awaited at the end, so its time overlaps the rest instead of preceding it. Still awaited before responding, so its result is reported rather than abandoned mid-flight.

## Safer — and this is the part worth reading

While checking what could be parallelised, I found an ordering constraint **nothing in the code stated**:

> `bookingSync`'s `markMeetingBooked()` moves a prospect who booked a call overnight to status `meeting_booked`.
> `autoQueueTopDrafts` selects on `READY_STATUSES`; `autoQueueDueFollowups` selects on `["contacted", "follow_up_sent"]`.

Run those concurrently and **someone who has already booked a call gets picked up for a cold first touch or a chase** — outreach sent hours after they booked. That's the class of send CLAUDE.md says costs a customer permanently.

The only thing preventing it today is statement order, and the existing comment only mentioned `autoQueue → send → brief` — so the dependency that actually bites was invisible. An obvious-looking *"wrap these in a `Promise.all`"* would have shipped it.

The chain is now documented as load-bearing and pinned by tests:

```
bookingSync → autoQueue → autoFollowups → emailAutopilot → brief
```

each `await`ed, with an explicit check that it's never gathered into a `Promise.all`.

## Verification

12 new tests, verified by re-breaking it **both** ways:

| Break | Result |
|---|---|
| Move `bookingSync` after `autoQueue` (the race) | **1 test fails** |
| Await the reminders inline (back on the critical path) | **4 fail** |

> The first attempt at that verification was vacuous — the revert script had a Python syntax error, so the tests passed against an unchanged file. Redone with the reverts actually applied.

- `npx vitest run` — **521 passed** (33 files)
- `npm run build` — green

## Regression guard

No migration. The send itself, the review gates, the inbound webhook and Jarvis are untouched — this changes **when two independent tasks run relative to each other**, not what any of them do. Authorisation still happens before any work.

Docs only. **Specified, not built** — privent-n8n owns the rig and costs it.

E4 has three sub-cells and exactly one is measured. **E4-c is green; `apiKey` and `tokenless` have never been run.** "E4 passes" is currently a sentence true of one third of E4.

Written at `d171f28` from the node's own code with every claim cited — this package has already shipped one version whose declared and actual contents disagreed.

## E4-c's green transfers to NEITHER, mechanically

| | detector set | who mints the token | FP filter |
|---|---|---|---|
| **E4-a** `apiKey` | core's **10** + org custom patterns + backend ML | **the backend** — `N8nHttpVault`, `/v1/vault/find-or-create-batch` | not applied |
| **E4-b** `tokenless` | core's **10** + backend ML via the visitor path | workflow static data | not applied |
| E4-c `local` | **575** generated detectors | workflow static data | **applied** |

Each row breaks the transfer on its own. And a green E4-a is a joint statement about this package **and a backend build** — the rig must record the backend SHA or the assertion has no subject.

## Negative controls, designed before the positive path

E4-c's controls do not transfer either: they work by making a **local detector** fail to see the value, and these two modes neither run those detectors nor apply that filter — all three would come back **masked** and prove nothing.

**NC-E4-a1, primary for both:** backend returns `200` with `entities: []` while the canary is a **person name or street address** — a kind the 10 core detectors do not carry. One response body, no fault injection in this package, and it reproduces the measured shape: in these modes **person and address are the backend's alone**.

## What each cannot see — now mandatory

**E4-b's is the sharp one:** tokenless emits **no audit event at all** (an anonymous visitor has no org). A rig asserting *"the block was visible to the operator"* must read the **item**, or it fails E4-b for a property that is by design.

**Both are blind to the vault contract** — NP-K covers 3 of 9 endpoints and the vault triple is not among them.

## The blocking property, stated as a finding

Both need **a backend process the runner can reach**. NP-K's three axes forbid it — no pullable image, private backend against a public repo, only `NPM_TOKEN`. **So E4-a and E4-b are Linux-box cells; E4-c is the single exception because it needs no backend at all.**

E4-a additionally needs an org and an org-scoped key **minted into a non-production database** — a hard precondition, recorded as one.

> A cell that cannot run is a finding. A cell that quietly is not run is the false green this programme has spent the week eliminating.

Recorded as `NP-AD`. Suggested order on measured cost: **E4-b first** (public endpoint, no org, no key), then E4-a.

author: adamaltman
body:
## What/Why/How?

**What:** Generated throw-mode clients can now return declared response headers. Passing `{ envelope: true }` on a call returns `{ data, headers, response }` instead of the parsed body alone.

**Why:** Throw mode (the default) returns only the body, so OpenAPI-declared success-response headers — `Pagination-Total`, rate limits, `Location` — were unreachable without switching the whole client to `--error-mode result`.

**How:**
- **IR:** operations carry `successResponseHeaders` built from the selected success response (including bodyless responses like `201` + `Location`); referenced scalar header schemas are dereferenced.
- **Runtime:** `execute` returns the envelope when `envelope === true`; header values are coerced to `number`/`boolean` per schema (blank/unparsable values are omitted, never `0`). Pagination iterators strip the flag so page pointers keep resolving against the body.
- **Types:** the `EnvelopeResult` conditional type keeps default call sites body-only (non-breaking) and narrows to `Envelope<…>` only for a literal `envelope: true`; a statically unknowable flag widens to the union. Result-mode clients ignore the option (they already return `response`).
- **Emitters:** header names become identifier-safe camelCase keys (`Pagination-Total` → `paginationTotal`, `3D-Secure` → `_3dSecure`) with deterministic collision suffixes; `<Op>ResponseHeaders` aliases are emitted; required headers are required properties (the type trusts the description, like body types).
- **Wrappers:** TanStack Query and SWR inits are `Omit<RequestOptions, 'envelope'>` and the forwarded calls strip the flag at runtime, so cached data is always the plain body. This also fixes a latent bug where grouped-style no-input SWR hooks passed `init` in the args slot.

## Reference

Closes #3001

## Testing

- New unit coverage across IR build, descriptor/alias/wrapper emitters, runtime coercion, and `EnvelopeResult` typing (993 client-generator tests).
- New e2e suite (`envelope.test.ts`) generates a client from a response-headers fixture and strict-tsc-checks envelope and default call sites; the TanStack e2e pins `useQuery(...).data` to the plain body type.
- Full suite: compile, typecheck, unit, e2e, lint, format all pass locally (one pre-existing `generator-contract` e2e failure in the local environment only; passes on CI from main).

Drive checkout, commit, and push through Git and assert the observable effects of all three installed hooks. body:
This PR enhances the accessibility of the application by addressing several missing keyboard affordances and screen reader labels on interactive elements:

1. **User Avatar Sign-Out (Dashboard):** The user avatar in the header is an `img` tag acting as a sign-out button. It has been updated with `role="button"`, `tabIndex={0}`, and `onKeyDown` handlers to support keyboard navigation (Enter and Space keys).
2. **Carousel Controls (PlaceDetail):** The left/right arrows and the indicator dots in the photo carousel are icon-only buttons. They now include descriptive `aria-label`s to inform screen reader users of their function.
3. **Modal Close Button (PlaceDetail):** The 'X' icon used to close the "Add Review" modal now has an `aria-label` ("Close modal").
4. **Learning Documented:** A new entry in `.jules/palette.md` has been added to document the importance of using proper semantic attributes for non-standard interactive elements and adding ARIA labels to icon-only buttons.

Test commands and mock server threads could outlive their fixtures, turning failures into hangs and allowing server state to race teardown. Give ordinary commands one deadline and recursive mock builds a longer one. Run each command in a process group or Windows job, terminate the whole tree on timeout, and bound captured-output cleanup. Cancel the mock server when its fixture drops and wait on a bounded completion handshake after its runtime and state are released. Retain the fixture directory if a pathological worker must be detached, and avoid a second panic while another failure unwinds. body:
Closes #3995.

The P1AM firmware owns the safety interlock, the four PID loops, and the analog/relay outputs — it is what keeps the plant safe when the Raspberry Pi host is gone. Nothing in CI compiled it and nothing ran its tests.

## What was already there, and why it stopped working

A host-side harness existed at `tests/p1am_control_system/firmware/`: a Makefile that builds the **real** firmware sources against a fake `HardwareInterface`, with assertions covering scaling, anti-windup, trip latching and NaN soft-fail. It sits inside a directory CI does collect (`ci-standard.yml:701` adds `tests/p1am_control_system/`) but holds no `.py` files, so pytest walked straight past it.

Never being run, it rotted until it no longer compiled:

- `MockHardware` did not implement `WriteHeaterRelay`, so the class was abstract and every `MockHardware hw;` was a hard error.
- The `StorageManager` round-trip still used the pre-lolo/hihi **4-argument** `Save`/`Load`; the real signature took 6 once `InterlockConfigData` grew to four limits (`kMagic` bumped 0xDC51 → 0xDC52).
- `TestSignalBroker` asserted 350 °C → 35.0 %, an expectation left over from a 1000 °C full scale. The firmware moved to 1400 °C, making the correct answer 25.0 %.

That last one is the interesting failure: the suite was not merely unbuilt, it encoded a **stale physical constant**. This is the class of drift the harness exists to catch.

## Changes

**Harness repair**
- `MockHardware` implements the full interface. It additionally records the highest value each analog output was ever commanded to, so a safety test can assert an output was *never energized* rather than merely reading zero at the end — the distinction that matters for the watchdog and E-stop work in #3999/#4002.
- The `StorageManager` test round-trips all four interlock tiers and asserts an untouched tag keeps its saved value, so a future struct change cannot silently drop lolo/hihi the way the last one did.
- `test_dcs.cpp` now `#error`s under `NDEBUG`. Every check in the suite is an `assert()`; a build that compiled them away would exit 0 having tested nothing.

**DRY fix that makes the stale assertion impossible to repeat**
- `kThermocoupleFullScaleC` moves from a function-local literal in `SignalBroker.cpp` to a public `static constexpr` in `SignalBroker.h`. The test derives its expected percentage from that constant instead of hardcoding one — hardcoding is exactly what let the assertion go stale. This also gives the backend cross-check in #3998 a single named definition to read against.

**CI**
- New `.github/workflows/p1am-firmware.yml`, path-filtered to the firmware and its tests, pinned to `[d-sorg-fleet, Linux]` (the pool is heterogeneous and the Makefile needs a POSIX toolchain):
  - `firmware-unit-tests` — plain `g++`, no board toolchain, runs in seconds. This is the TDD vehicle for the rest of the firmware cluster.
  - `firmware-compile` — `arduino-cli` against the real `P1AM-100:samd` package, catching library and signature breakage the host harness cannot see (it never includes `P1AM.h` or `Ethernet.h`).
- The unit-test job greps the binary's own success line rather than trusting the exit code, so a build that silently tested nothing still fails.
- Toolchain versions are written to the job summary each run, so a firmware binary can be traced to the toolchain that produced it.

**Housekeeping**
- `.gitignore` for `*.o`, `test_dcs`, and `config.bin` (StorageManager persists to it when exercised on the host), so a local `make test` cannot dirty the tree.

## Verification

Built and run under WSL Ubuntu-22.04, g++ 11.4:

```
=== DCS CORE FIRMWARE TDD TEST RUNNER ===
TestSignalBroker PASSED!
TestPIDController PASSED!
TestSafetyInterlock PASSED!
TestStorageManager PASSED!
TestSoftFailRuntimeContracts PASSED!
All C++ Core Firmware Tests Passed Successfully!
```

No Python or frontend code is touched.

## Follow-on

This PR deliberately does **not** fix any firmware behaviour — it only makes the firmware testable and gated. The defects the harness now protects against are next, each with a failing test written first:

- #3999 comms watchdog
- #4001 trip tier, unrouted tags, `ClearTrip` reachability
- #4002 PID integral reset on setpoint change
- #4032 tag clamp versus interlock limit domain

One gap this PR exposes and does not close: `SafetyInterlock::Evaluate` reads only `high_limits_`/`low_limits_`, and the harness only ever exercised those — nothing tests the HIHI/LOLO tier because nothing evaluates it. That is #4001's job.

body:
Closes #296. Part of #295.

The Caller's Box writes "balance an existing wave" as its own figure line — `(4) Balance wave of four (NR,WL)`, `(4) Balance long wave (NR, women face in)`. That is **4,613 lines across the 24,107-dance corpus**, the single largest `custom` bucket. This PR models them.

There is **no `balance_the_wave` move and none is added.** The taxonomy expresses "a wave exists and is balanced" as the wave-**formation** move carrying its `balance` flag, so such a line maps onto that move as **one figure keeping its own beats** — never an extra 0-beat form figure.

## 👀 Two things to see before the detail

**1. ~2,700 imported figures change how they READ.** Lines that today display as
the verbatim text `Balance wave of four (NR,WL)` will display as
`form short waves - role2s by the left in the center, neighbor by the right on
the sides - and balance`. That is the ratified model (a balanced wave *is* the
formation move carrying its balance), and the hands/roles are preserved rather
than dropped — but it is a **visible wording change for callers** and belongs in
the release notes. Worth a conscious sign-off rather than discovering it in the
UI. The move's own label also changes: **"form a wave" → "form short waves"**.

**2. Cross-unit API change: `_tcbPassPeople` → `tcbPassPeople` (now public).**
The wave-annotation decoder reads the same TCB people codes the hey and
grand-right-and-left decoders do, so it reuses that one map instead of
duplicating it (#712 extended it with `P1`/`S1`/`S2` days ago). It lives in
`callersbox_figure_dialect.dart`, which the **gate unit is also editing right
now** — flagging so reviewers see the rename named rather than meeting it in a
conflict.

## ⚠️ This PR ships a schema migration (18 → 19)

`form_a_short_wave` is **renamed** `form_short_waves`, and a taxonomy rename is a migration, not an additive change: stored figures carry the old move id.

`CompendiumDatabase` **schema v19** rewrites `move` in every `dances.figures_json` blob — **including sides nested inside a `meanwhile` container**, which the schema-v18 `allemande_orbit` rewrite can itself produce. It follows the v12 ocean-wave / v18 orbit precedent exactly: per-row and per-figure parse-never-throw, anything unmappable or malformed left **byte-identical** (riding the non-destructive unknown-move path, #358), and a derived rebuild scheduled **only when a figure actually changed**.

Blast radius to review:

- `dance_figures.canonicalText` and `dance_fts` change for affected figures — this is the sanctioned canonical-changing migration, and the rebuild marker handles it.
- The historical v12 step still writes the **old** id (frozen history), so a long hop from ≤ v11 lands on `form_a_short_wave` at v12 and is renamed at v19. There is a **v11 → v19 chained-upgrade test** asserting exactly that.
- New `test/storage/fixtures/v18.sqlite` + `generate_v18_fixture.dart` + migration tests (CI's `tools/ci/check_schema_migration.py` gate passes locally).
- **No alias** is left behind for the old id — in-code references must use the new one. The pre-rename label survives as a `searchKeyword`, so the picker still finds it.

## Taxonomy v21

- **Rename** `form_a_short_wave` → `form_short_waves`, display label **"form short waves"** (was "form a wave"). The figure is the whole set's short waves, and every TCB wording is "wave of four" / "short waves".
- **`form_long_waves` gains `whom` + `hand` + `balance`.** TCB states all three on the line (`Balance long wave (NR, women face in)` = *neighbours by the right, women facing in*) on ~1,500 corpus lines; ContraDB's `formLongWavesWords` models only the facing. `whom`/`hand` therefore default to the `unspecified` sentinel (the v20 `mad_robin.whom` precedent) and `balance` to `false`.
- **`renderTemplate` is unchanged for both moves**, so the new `whom`/`hand`/`balance` params are byte-stable: at their sentinel/`false` defaults a figure renders exactly as it did at v20 (test-enforced). The **rename** is deliberately *not* byte-stable, and the two halves drive different machinery — the move **id** change is what forces the schema-v19 migration (an unmigrated figure would stop resolving and fall to the #358 raw-id fallback), while the **`displayName`** change is what forces the derived rebuild, since `{move}` expands the display name (`FigureRenderer._renderMoveName` uses the id only as a dialect-substitution lookup key). Renaming just the id would have needed the migration but not the rebuild.
- `form_a_long_wave` is **untouched**; `form_rings` is explicitly **out of scope**.

### On `who` — a conflict I escalated rather than guessed

The requested display template was `form long waves - {whom} by the {hand}, {who} facing out`. But `who` already means the pair that faces **IN** (ContraDB `formLongWavesWords`, and our current render "…{who} face in, {other} face out") — and TCB states the same fact. Rendering `{who} facing out` literally would have **inverted the displayed meaning of every stored ContraDB-imported figure**.

Resolved with the maintainer: `who` keeps its facing-IN meaning (no reinterpretation of stored data, no `who` migration), and the display line becomes

```
form long waves - {whom} by the {hand}, {who} facing in, {other} facing out{ - and balance}
```

with the hold clause emitted only when **both** `whom` and `hand` are stated.

## Issue #296 (display path)

Both wave-formation moves now append a ` - and balance` clause when balanced; previously `form_short_waves` dropped the flag entirely and `form_long_waves` had no flag. `form_a_long_wave` and `pass_the_ocean` already embedded their balance and are unchanged. The wave moves stay deliberately absent from the generic "balance &" prefix table — listing them would double the clause. All of it is `!forCanonical`-gated.

Note that **#296's reference to `form_an_ocean_wave` is stale**: that MoveDef was split at taxonomy v13 and *removed* at v14 (migrated by schema v12). The work lands on `form_short_waves` and `form_long_waves` instead; the docs say so explicitly.

## Import: how nothing gets stolen

The balance line still parses to `custom`. The mapping is a **final pass of the CallersBox cross-line merge** (`_promoteBalanceWaveLines`), so by construction it only ever sees leftovers:

1. **Fold 1 (forward)** — a balance line before a swing / petronella / rory o'more / box the gnat / swat the flea / box circulate folds into that move, exactly as before. ~44% of balance-wave lines have such a successor.
2. **Fold 4 (backward, #577)** — a balance-wave line after a structured wave move folds into it with beats summed, so an explicitly-formed-then-balanced wave yields **one** form figure. `form_long_waves` joins that set now that it has a `balance` flag. The balance line's annotation additionally **enriches** the merged figure with any hand/pair the forming line did not state, instead of being discarded.
3. **Promotion** — whatever is left becomes the form figure on its own (the implicit case: an allemande leaves the dancers in the wave the very next line balances).

A promotion is **skipped** when the preceding figure is a still-custom wave-*forming* line, so a form figure is never emitted beside an unstructured "form …" line.

### Latent gap found and fixed

`form wave of four` never recognized, so the "explicit prior forming" merge **silently could not fire for short waves** — `Circle right 3/4; form wave of four` stayed whole-custom. `form (a) wave of four [with <dancer>]` (TCB's dominant forming wording, ~1,000 clauses; the `with` tail sets `sides`) now structures.

### Decoding the annotation

The parenthetical is the wave's payload, not a droppable note — structuring the line without it would *destroy* detail the custom text preserved verbatim. So:

| line shape | maps to |
| --- | --- |
| `Balance wave of four (<pair><H>, <role><H'>)` | `form_short_waves{balance, sides, center, centerHand}` |
| `Balance wave of four` (no annotation) | `form_short_wa

Two phases. **Phase 3 is complete. Phase 4-i is not** — its backend is finished and tested, but live sync does not yet work in a browser. Details and a recommendation at the bottom.

Collaboration is off unless `Y_SWEET_CONNECTION_STRING` is set, so merging this changes nothing about how the app behaves today.

## Phase 3 — version history (complete)

Every document keeps earlier drafts. Open one, click **History**, preview a version, restore it. Restoring is itself snapshotted, so restoring the wrong draft is undoable, and it updates the editor in place rather than reloading.

No migration was needed — `document_versions` has existed since Phase 1 and had never been written to.

**When a version is written**, which is the design's core:

- the document has no history yet, **or**
- the newest version is more than five minutes old, **or**
- **a different author is saving than last time.**

That third rule is the one the feature exists for. Two collaborators overwriting each other is exactly what history rescues, and time-bucketing alone would let one silently replace the other inside a single window. Autosave fires roughly every 800ms, so snapshotting every save would put hundreds of full-document JSONB copies per session into a free-tier database.

Each document keeps its newest 50, pruned in the same transaction as the insert so retention cannot drift. Title-only changes record nothing. The row holds the content being *replaced*, which is what makes restore mean "go back".

**Worth a reviewer's eye:** every version lookup filters on the document id *as well as* the version id. Matching the version alone would make `/documents/A/versions/{id-from-B}` a way to read B's content through A's permissions. The test for it uses a caller who owns both documents, so it cannot pass for permission reasons.

## Phase 4-i — live collaboration (backend complete, sync unfinished)

**Transport: [y-sweet](https://github.com/jamsocket/y-sweet)**, chosen after checking the alternatives. Liveblocks documents only a Node SDK for issuing tokens, which would have meant a Next.js route handler holding the vendor secret — reintroducing the server-side-in-Next arrangement Phase 2C-iii deleted. y-sweet has a Python SDK, so the function that checks `can_view` and the function that mints the room token are the same one. It is also MIT and self-hostable, so the vendor is replaceable rather than load-bearing, and it runs locally, so this costs nothing to develop.

**Done:** `POST /api/v1/documents/{id}/collab` checks access *before* minting, derives the room id from the document id server-side, returns `enabled: false` when unconfigured rather than erroring, and maps an unreachable server to 503 — never 401.

y-sweet supports **read-only tokens**, which its guides do not show and its SDK helper never requests. Asking for one directly means a viewer's token is refused writes *by the server*, not merely by the browser.

Implements the **Party Mode** handoff: two friends team up on separate devices, then meet people together — a solo stranger (room of 3) or another party (room of 4). Solo 1-on-1 is preserved.

> ⚠️ **Please test with real devices before merging.** The server room logic and client state machine are unit-/integration-tested, but the multi-peer **mesh video** can only be exercised with real cameras across tabs/devices (can't run headless).

## What changed
Moved from a single-partner model to a **room + WebRTC mesh** model on both sides.

**Server (`server.js`)**
- Stable `peerId` per socket. A **party** = a durable group of 1 (solo) or 2 (joined by 4-char code); a **session** = two matched parties (2–4 people). Matchmaking pairs *parties* (1+1, 2+1, 2+2).
- Mesh signaling: `peer-join{peerId,initiator,friend}` / `peer-leave`, `signal{to}` routed with `from`; deterministic initiator (smaller peerId) avoids glare. `chat` broadcasts to the room.
- `next` dissolves the session and returns each party to matchmaking **intact**; a **re-match cooldown** stops you instantly re-pairing with who you just skipped.
- Region/language + interest filters, IP bans, and fail-safe client moderation all preserved.
- **Solo-vs-solo is just a 2-person mesh — identical to the old 1-on-1 flow.**

**Client (`public/index.html`)**
- `Map<peerId, RTCPeerConnection>` + a dynamic remote-tile grid keyed by peerId; your camera stays as its own tile. Per-**stranger** report flags (friends aren't reportable).
- Party UI: **Create / Join** (code), a waiting view, **Find people**, **Leave**. The solo **Start** path is untouched. Chat, interests, filters, moderation, Skip/Stop all work in the room.
- WebRTC calls are wrapped in try/catch so one failed peer connection can't take down the whole room.

## Testing done
- **Server (fake WS clients):** solo→2-mesh, party+solo=room of 3 (each sees 2 peers), party+party=room of 4 (each sees 3), Next keeps friends together + drops the stranger, chat broadcast, `signal` routing with `from`, report/ban. All green.
- **Client (in-browser):** create→code→friend joins→matched→stranger tile→Stop-back-to-party, correct actions/flags/chat per state, **zero console errors**.
- **Not tested:** live mesh video across real devices — the thing to check before merging (open 3–4 tabs/devices: solo↔solo, a party of 2, party+solo=3, party+party=4, Next, Report).

author: valkomen-llc
body:
## Por qué unas escenas cobraban vida y otras no

**No era que el motor fallara en unas y acertara en otras.** Las tres pasaban por KIE. Lo que ocurría es que el control de calidad **descartaba** algunas y las sustituía por `resolveSceneWithStillMotion` — la foto quieta con desplazamiento de encuadre, que es la firma exacta de lo reportado: *«se mueve de un lado a otro»*.

La ruta, verificada en el código:

1. La escena nace con `attempts = 0`; el primer despacho **no** lo incrementa.
2. Falla la fidelidad → `sc.attempts < 1` → `relaunchScene` → `attempts = 1`.
3. Vuelve a fallar → `sc.analysis?.hasPeople && sc.attempts >= 1` → **2.5D**.
4. Ya convertida, el rescate de escenas congeladas la excluye (`sc.engine !== 'still_motion'`): **irreversible**.

Dos escenas de tres siguiendo ese camino dan exactamente el Reel descrito. Y cada una consumió créditos de video **dos veces** antes de ser descartada.

## El criterio se volvía contra el objetivo

Una escena que cobra **más** vida se parece **menos** a la foto de origen —cabezas giradas, manos en otra posición—, así que es la **más propensa** a suspender la fidelidad.

Se estaba castigando justo lo que el módulo busca producir, y reemplazándolo por lo que no busca. Lo señalé como riesgo al bajar el piso estructural en v4.673; era el mismo mecanismo, un escalón más arriba.

## Qué cambia

El clip animado **se conserva siempre**. Lo que se aparta de la fotografía se marca `needs_review` con su nota, y la decisión de rehacerlo es del usuario — que es quien puede mirar el video. Una medición de similitud no puede juzgar si una cabeza girada está *bien* girada.

**Excepción:** `brandAltered` y `textIllegible` se siguen regenerando solos. Son los defectos que descalifican una pieza institucional y no admiten criterio estético.

El respaldo 2.5D **no se elimina**: queda para la elección expresa del estilo «Fotográfico», que es lo que siempre fue. Y la línea de tiempo ahora **dice** qué escena se resolvió sin IA, en vez de que parezca una escena normal que no se movió.

## Efecto secundario deseable

Deja de gastarse una segunda ronda de créditos de video en escenas que iban a acabar descartadas de todos modos.

## Comprobado

- `npm run build` verde.
- `tsc -p tsconfig.app.json`: **331 errores, los mismos que en `main`**.
- El controlador carga y el frontend compila sin errores propios.

## Lo que sigue sin poder afirmarse

Que las tres escenas cobren vida depende de lo que entregue Kling. Lo que esta versión garantiza es que **si el motor animó una escena, esa escena llega al Reel** — antes podía animarla bien y ser reemplazada por un paneo. El `Nivel de vida` de v4.675 sigue detectando y relanzando lo que el motor deje realmente congelado.

author: alphaonedev
body:
Closes #2578
Closes #2581
Closes #2582
Closes #2585

Four postgres read-path defects. **Every claim below was reproduced by EXECUTION against the live certified tier (PG 18.4 + AGE 1.7.0 + pgvector 0.8.6, 8,724-row corpus) before any code was written.** Two of the four issues' own framings turned out to be wrong and are corrected here; one index the issues asked for is **deliberately not shipped** because measuring it showed a regression.

### Evidence discipline

The development host was running six concurrent audit lanes at load ~20 on 14 cores. Every headline number below is therefore anchored to a **load-independent** signal — `EXPLAIN` plan shape, buffer counts, rows read, statement counts, wire bytes — and wall-clock figures are labelled indicative. The regression tests assert **shape, never wall-clock**: a latency threshold in CI is a flake generator that proves nothing about the mechanism.

---

## #2578 — the v56 composite list indexes never landed on postgres (schema v87 → v88)

`migrate_v56()` was recorded as a postgres version-stamp no-op, so for the whole v56..v87 range a namespace-scoped `list` read **every row in the namespace and sorted it** — O(namespace size) where SQLite is O(limit).

| shape | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| ns-scoped `LIMIT 10` | **1,880 buffers**, 7,855 rows read, top-N heapsort | **8 buffers**, 10 rows read, **no sort node** |
| ns-scoped `LIMIT 1000` (`load_family`) | 2,079 buffers | 321 buffers |
| `list_archived`, cold tenant, generic plan | 47.912 ms, 180,000 rows filtered | 0.062 ms, `Index Cond` |

**Scope stated honestly:** the win is proportional to namespace size (a 10-row namespace measures no win and no loss), and it is contingent on postgres keeping a *custom* plan — forced generic, the composite is not chosen and the win is zero. Extra filters (`tier`/`agent_id`/`since`/`until`/`valid_at`) do **not** regress; the planner declines the composite and both index sets converge.

`list_archived` also needed the #1473 sargable split, or the new archive index is unusable under the generic plan sqlx settles into — without it the index would have been pure write amplification for zero read benefit.

### The unscoped index is deliberately WITHHELD (against the issue and against SQLite parity)

It was in the first draft; an adversarial re-measurement removed it. With most of a namespace expired-but-not-yet-GC'd (an ordinary steady state — GC runs every 30 min), its presence makes the planner **abandon the scoped composite and walk across ALL namespaces**:

| index set | buffers | rows filtered |
|---|---|---|
| before (none) | 1,989 | 7,000, in-namespace |
| **ns-scoped only (shipped)** | **1,854** | 6,882, in-namespace |
| both | **3,041** | **9,621, across all namespaces** |

Its only benefit is the rarer unscoped `list` (0.58 ms absolute) against permanent write amplification. Filed as #2610 with the evidence rather than shipped on parity grounds, and pinned by a test so it cannot be reintroduced silently.

### A plain in-transaction `CREATE INDEX` here would have been a fleet-wide BOOT BRICK

This is the finding I'd most want reviewed. Pooled connections carry `statement_timeout = 30s` + `lock_timeout = 5s` from `after_connect`; `connect_*` clears them **only on the dedicated advisory-lock connection**, never on the connection a migrate arm's `pool.begin()` uses. Reproduced live with **one ordinary uncommitted `INSERT`** open:

```
ERROR:  canceling statement due to lock timeout
Time: 5002.006 ms
```

The arm's tx rolls back → version not stamped → `migrate_locked` returns `Err` → `connect()` returns `Err` → **the daemon cannot boot**, identically on every retry while any writer is active. This is **concurrency-driven, not size-driven**: it fires on an 8k-row table as readily as a 3-billion-row one. The same probe with `CONCURRENTLY` and timeouts cleared waited the writer out and succeeded, leaving `indisvalid = t`.

So the arm builds `CONCURRENTLY`, on a dedicated connection, outside any transaction, with `lock_timeout` cleared and `statement_timeout` **bounded** (an unbounded wait would hang `connect()` past a supervisor's start deadline and turn a clean wait into a crash-loop), **fail-open** (these indexes are derived, disposable, non-UNIQUE data — refusing a fleet's boot over a missing perf index trades total availability for zero integrity), and **self-healing**: the same idempotent helper re-runs on every connect, probing `pg_index.indisvalid` rather than mere existence, because `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF NOT EXISTS` silently no-ops over an INVALID leftover that the planner ignores while postgres still maintains it on every write.

The v57 arm has the same latent hazard and is filed as #2614.

---

## #2581 — the recall ledger was O(limit) in round trips

`BEGIN` + one INSERT **per candidate** + `COMMIT`, on a recall that is otherwise pure since #1869/P0-1. Now one `INSERT … SELECT … FROM UNNEST(…) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`: **`2 + limit` statements → 1**, which is the structural, load-independent claim.

Honest magnitudes, measured over the **prepared protocol** (what sqlx uses) inside one transaction: **limit=10 8.04 → 3.89 ms (−52%)**, **limit=50 21.75 → 5.40 ms (−75%)**, marginal 0.36–0.45 ms/row — consistent with the **0.19 ms/row** #2581 itself measured against a real daemon. **An earlier draft of this PR claimed 4.8×/16.4×; that was wrong.** Those came from a `psql` harness whose simple-protocol autocommit made each statement its own WAL fsync (3.5 ms/row) — measuring N fsyncs where the daemon pays one per recall. The issue's own instrumented number was the more trustworthy one and it is now cited as the corroborating datum.

Rows are **byte-identical**: same columns, values, `folded = FALSE`, `observed_at`, `ON CONFLICT` disposition, atomicity, and returned count of rows actually inserted. Intra-batch first-wins verified live. `UNNEST` over four arrays rather than multi-row `VALUES` because `candidates` is bounded by `LIST_MAX_LIMIT`: a `VALUES` form emits ~5k bind parameters and a *different* SQL string per candidate count, thrashing sqlx's statement cache one order of magnitude below the protocol's 65535-parameter ceiling. A comment and a test pin that this must never become `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, which raises `21000` on the very input the loop accepted — a hard failure on an append-only audit surface.

---

## #2582 — the AGE branch has never once succeeded on the pinned AGE version

`build_find_paths_current_view_cypher` emits `ALL(e IN relationships(p) WHERE …)`, and **AGE 1.7.0 rejects it at parse time** (`syntax error at or near "("`) — reproduced against both a scratch graph and the live `memory_graph`. `ALL`/`ANY`/`NONE` are grammar keywords there, not callable functions. So every call paid `BEGIN` + `LOAD 'age'` + `SET LOCAL search_path` + a failing parse + a rollback + a per-call WARN, then ran the CTE anyway.

`find_paths` now routes to the CTE unconditionally. **Zero answers change** — 100% of production AGE results already came from the CTE. Gone: the wasted round trips, and a WARN firing on every single call that buried the real `age_substrate_unreachable` signal it resembles.

**Fixing the Cypher would have been the wrong repair.** On a purpose-built 20,003-vertex / 60,000-edge graph, a *parseable* depth-4 traversal returning 120 rows costs **987.8 ms**, and its plan is a Nested Loop whose outer side is a `Seq Scan` over all 20,003 vertices with 2,400,240 rows removed by `age_match_vle_terminal_edge`. Cost scales with |V|, not depth, so no depth K favours AGE and the crossover recedes as a corpus grows. A GIN vertex-property index does not rescue it (987.8 → 979 ms).

**Honest comparison:** an earlier draft quoted 877× against a simplified *directed* CTE production does not run. Like-for-like against the actual `find_paths_cte` (undirected, visited-path array): **987.8 vs 462.99 ms — 2.1×**. The AGE path being dead code means it was never a live latency cost, only wasted

## Review finding A1 (live security hole)

Live `pg_proc` ACLs show seven `devnet_*` functions carrying the default PUBLIC execute grant, making them callable by **anon** through PostgREST with just the publishable key. Six are SECURITY DEFINER; `devnet_transform_sales` alone can rewrite sale facts, delete `sale_parcel` rows on drift, and null `validated_at`.

Affected: `devnet_transform_sales`, `devnet_transform_sale_notes`, `devnet_transform_tif_registry`, `devnet_transform_pp_waivers`, `devnet_transform_correction_abatement`, `devnet_geometry_retire_mislinked(boolean, date)`, `devnet_claim_export_request(text)`.

Root cause: migrations run as a role not covered by the 2026-07-06 default-privileges hardening, so functions without an explicit revoke ship with PUBLIC execute. `devnet_claim_export_request` even had a revoke — but only for `anon, authenticated`; the `=X` PUBLIC grant survived.

The migration revokes from public/anon/authenticated, grants service_role (zero behavior change — the pipeline is the only legitimate caller), and pins `pg_temp` last in `devnet_transform_sales`''s search_path.

⚠️ **Not yet applied live** — the MCP apply was blocked by the permission classifier. Needs a one-time approved `apply_migration` (or SQL-editor paste), then `npm run db:sync-applied` and the ACL verification query.

author: fredm237
body:
## Le symptôme

En production, `/api/catalog/stats` renvoyait :

```json
{"offers":791119,"products":229370,"products_multi_merchant":26156,"offers_linked":1000}
```

229 370 produits créés, mais **1 000 offres rattachées** — exactement la taille d'un lot. Le rattachement ne dépassait jamais le premier lot.

## La cause

Une requête `UPDATE` par produit. À cette échelle, ~230 000 allers-retours séquentiels vers la base. Le catalogue avait été multiplié par huit depuis l'écriture du code (95 k → 791 k offres) et l'implémentation ne tenait plus.

## Les correctifs

| Étape | Avant | Après |
|---|---|---|
| Création des produits | un `flush()` par produit | insertion groupée + relecture des ids |
| Mise à jour des produits | un `UPDATE` par produit | table Core + `bindparam`, par lots |
| Rattachement des offres | un `UPDATE` par produit | bulk update by primary key, par lots |

Deux subtilités rencontrées :
- L'`UPDATE` groupé avec `WHERE` déclenche `InvalidRequestError` tant que l'ORM tente de synchroniser ses objets → `synchronize_session=None`.
- Pour les offres, la forme idiomatique est le *bulk update by primary key* (dicts contenant `id`) ; pour les produits, la clé est l'EAN et non la PK, d'où le passage par la table Core.

`offers_linked` est ajouté au bilan renvoyé.

## Vérification à l'échelle

Le bug étant un problème d'échelle, il est vérifié à l'échelle — pas sur six lignes :

```
35 034 offres · 20 000 produits · 9 998 multi-marchands
Durée : 1,3 s
offers_linked en base : 35 034 / 35 034
```

Le contrôle porte sur le compte **réel en base**, pas sur la valeur renvoyée par la fonction.

25 tests passent.

## Après merge

```bash
curl -X POST -H "x-admin-token: <ADMIN_SYNC_TOKEN>" \
  "https://<backend>/api/catalog/admin/rebuild-products"
```

`offers_linked` doit alors monter bien au-delà de 1 000.

body:
## Summary

Backend core of the file-backed Kanban board — Phase 1, slice 1 of 3 (backend only; the browser UI is slice 2). It's a Node process that reads/writes one Markdown file per task under a repo-root `tasks/` directory, exposes a REST API, and broadcasts external file changes over a WebSocket. Loopback-only.

Built TDD, one commit per task.

## Tasks

- **T-0010** — scaffold `tools/board` (Vite + Vitest + ESLint flat config, npm scripts, smoke test)
- **T-0011** — task Markdown parser/serializer (YAML frontmatter ↔ Task object; round-trip, malformed, missing-field and unicode tests)
- **T-0012** — `TaskStore` interface + `FsTaskStore` over `tasks/*.md` (list/get/create/update/move, **atomic writes** via temp-file + rename, id-collision reject)
- **T-0013** — gap-tolerant `T-NNNN` id allocator that **never reuses** an id, even after deletion (high-water mark persisted in gitignored `tasks/.id-allocator.json`)
- **T-0014** — REST API `GET/POST/PATCH /api/tasks` (raw `node:http`, validation rejects → 4xx)
- **T-0015** — `TaskWatcher` (chokidar) + `WsHub` broadcast on `/ws/board` (an external edit to a `tasks/*.md` file emits a change event)

## Tests & checks

- **83 tests across 9 files, all green**; ESLint flat config clean; `vite build` succeeds (placeholder UI entry for T-0016).
- Also smoke-tested against the real dev server (create/list/patch + external-edit broadcast), scratch files cleaned up.

## Invariants honored

- **Binds 127.0.0.1 only** (HTTP + WS share a single listener via `noServer` + manual upgrade routing; it throws if a non-loopback host is passed — no `0.0.0.0` anywhere in `src/`).
- Atomic file writes; ids never reused; one Markdown file per task; ESM throughout; no auth/multi-user (out of scope for Phase 1).

## How to run

```bash
cd tools/board && npm install && npm run dev   # http://127.0.0.1:4173  (ws: /ws/board)

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:4173/api/tasks -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"title":"Example","phase":1}'
curl http://127.0.0.1:4173/api/tasks
curl -X PATCH http://127.0.0.1:4173/api/tasks/T-0001 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"status":"ready"}'
# WS: connect ws://127.0.0.1:4173/ws/board, then create/edit/delete a tasks/*.md file and watch the broadcast
```

## Notes / decisions

- Raw `node:http` (no Express) per the "minimal framework" rule; tests hit a real server via Node's built-in `fetch`.
- Bumped `vite`/`vitest` to clear a moderate esbuild dev-server audit advisory.
- `POST /api/tasks` defaults `priority`→`P2`, `status`→`backlog`, `created`→today; only `title` and `phase` are required.

## Reviewer checklist

- [ ] Backend runs; the curl flow behaves
- [ ] Loopback-only bind is acceptable
- [ ] Good to merge into `develop`

Base: `develop` ← `feature/phase-1-board-core`. Part of Phase 1 (option b: three grouped PRs). Slice 2 = board UI (T-0016–T-0017), slice 3 = PTY terminal + dependency guards (T-0018–T-0019).

author: lingelo
body:
## Pourquoi

Le produit promettait plus large qu'il ne pouvait tenir — un périmètre France et un mode Monde sans données opérationnelles, un onglet Données alimenté par un script capable de publier un historique amputé en silence. Cette PR resserre le périmètre sur ce que les services publient réellement, et corrige les défauts constatés en session.

Règle appliquée aux retraits : **un périmètre ne figure dans l'interface que si un service en publie les sinistres.**

## Retraits

- **Périmètre France** — aucun flux public ne publie les interventions des SDIS en temps réel (BDIFF et Prométhée sont des archives, feuxdeforet.fr agrège des signalements citoyens derrière une convention).
- **Mode Monde**, liste des foyers satellite et tuiles associées. La couche reste accessible partout en calque, via le menu des fonds de carte.
- **Onglet Données**, hook, script d'agrégation et étapes de cache du workflow. Le script publiait un historique amputé avec un **code de sortie 0** quand une archive échouait.
- **Dictionnaire français** — ni la France ni un public francophone ne sont couverts.

Le motif de chaque retrait est consigné dans le code. Titre et méta-description, qui annonçaient encore « Portugal, Spain and France » et « Iberia and worldwide », sont corrigés.

## Corrections

| Défaut | Cause |
|---|---|
| Andalousie « indisponible » | Réponse INFOCA tronquée servie par le cache de Chrome (commit dédié) |
| Géolocalisation muette | L'échec recadrait la carte sans un mot |
| Panneau des sources invisible | `z-[400]` sur un élément `static` + `overflow-x-auto` qui clippe |
| Bande vide au repli | Leaflet n'écoute que `window.resize`, jamais son conteneur |
| Loupe décentrée de 7 px | Champ de 30 px contre un bouton de 38 px |
| « 1 sinistres », statut non traduit | Accord et libellé des notifications |
| Alertes silencieuses une fois l'onglet fermé | La limite est désormais **dite** : sans service worker, rien n'est émis en arrière-plan |

## Interface

- Les filtres de la liste gouvernent **aussi la carte** — prédicat unique dans `lib/filters.ts`, appliqué en amont, pour que les deux vues ne puissent plus se contredire.
- Filtre « en cours » par défaut, visible et réversible.
- Fond topographique par défaut, atténué, avec un `maxZoom` par couche.
- Couche satellite en **braise** graduée par fraîcheur, animée par les deux canvas et non par les 80 000 foyers. La gamme reste sous le spectre chaud vif des statuts, pour qu'une détection ne se lise pas comme un sinistre confirmé.
- Menu des fonds de carte ouvert au **clic** — au survol, il était inatteignable au doigt.
- Colonne de gauche repliable sur desktop.

## Vérifications

CI rejouée en local depuis un état propre : `npm ci` (0 vulnérabilité), `npm run lint`, `npm run build:data` (142 064 foyers, 250 incidents, **4/4 services**), `npm run build`. Bundle 457 → 434 kB.

Parcours alertes testé de bout en bout dans le navigateur : création de zone, persistance, détection dans le rayon, heures calmes, et notification émise (permission simulée).

body:
PR IV of the fifteenth improvement plan: the terminal envelope conformance table (RV1106), part B of the P1-5 judge item.

## What

- `packages/cli/src/envelope-conformance.test.ts`: ONE truth table drives every terminal path (ok, error, exhausted, cancelled, superseded) on the real engine, twice per row with identical fixtures: through the SDK (resolved outcome, `run:end`, the OTel export over the same stream and result) and over HTTP (POST /runs, the terminal `GET /runs/:id` body, the SSE replay). Every surface reading is checked against the SAME expected row, so a divergence between any two surfaces is a red test, and the table is the anchor future terminal fields extend.
- The table pins the surface honesty rules beside the facts: `handle.result` rejects typed on an unsettled terminal (RV907); `GET /runs/:id` serves the typed wire error for a rejected segment with no envelope (the `settled: false` envelopes exist only on the event stream); the OTel run span refuses green and names WHICH refusal ended it; the `run:end` siblings keep their byte contracts (absent-means-settled, absent-means-exact) against the envelope's normalized booleans.
- The red-first fix the table found: `toOtel` awaited `run.result` after its export loop, so a superseded or settlement-outage terminal failed the WHOLE export with the typed rejection even though the stream had already carried the refusal and every span was correctly closed. The leftover-close now settles on the result either way: a rejecting `result` never fails a completed export, and a leftover span from a stream truncated before `run:end` refuses green.
- Docs: the observability envelope section documents the conformance contract.

## Evidence

- Red first: the superseded row and the truncated-stream unit were red on v1.141.0 (`toOtel` rethrew the rejection); the other rows pin the observed contracts (an exhausted terminal whose call landed carries no error; a call that died without a usage report reads `usageApprox: true` with its model keyed at zero in the split).

author: reynoldsproductions
body:
Preserves work that until now only existed on a local machine (plan file, scratch scripts in `/tmp`, and knowledge that was only in a chat transcript).

## Why

While testing against a real Eos console we found several behaviours that **contradict ETC's published OSC documentation**. One of them — colour argument scaling — would have silently broken every colour in the planned web UI. None of it was written down anywhere durable.

## What's here

### `docs/eos-osc-findings.md`
Behaviour verified against a live console (Eos v3.3.9.25):

| Finding | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| **Colour args are 0–100, not 0–1** | Docs say `0.0–1.0`. Proved by read-back: `rgb [0,0,1]` → Blue **16.38**; `rgb [0,100,0]` → Green **100**. Building to the docs makes everything nearly black. |
| **Parameter ranges are self-describing** | `/eos/get/params/<chan>` returns `(name, current, min, max)` per param — `Hue 0–360`, `Strobe 0–255`, `Dimmer Curve 0–9`. Build controls from these; don't hardcode. |
| **Live parameter push exists** | `/eos/subscribe/param`, `/eos/out/active/wheel/*`, `/eos/out/color/hs` all push real values. Earlier assumption that only optimistic echo was possible was wrong. |
| **Cue lists aren't numbered from 1** | Test show's only list is **99**. `/eos/get/cue/1/count` → 0. Always enumerate. |
| **Empty index queries return malformed stubs** | `/eos/get/cue/99/index/0` on an empty list replies `/eos/out/get/cue/0/0` with no UID. Parsers must reject these. |
| **Magic sheets are metadata-only** | `[index, uid, label]` — no geometry. A third-party "magic sheet" view must define its own layout. |
| **`/eos/out/user` echoes only on change** | Re-claiming the current user is silent, so absence is not an error. |

Also documents why Companion is unaffected (it's TCP 3032; we're UDP — disjoint transports) and two VPN-related failures that looked exactly like OSC bugs.

### `tools/diagnostics/`
Four reusable read-only probes, console address from `EOS_HOST`. All verified against real hardware:

- `probe.mjs` — reachability and return path, exits non-zero on no feedback
- `inventory.mjs` — show contents, with cue lists enumerated properly
- `params.mjs <chan>` — live values and real min/max per parameter
- `capture.mjs` — record raw output to build fixtures

### `test/fixtures/eos-out.json`
30 real captured messages for the parser tests that the web UI work will need, including the malformed-stub and empty-args variants. Show file path scrubbed.

### `docs/plans/web-ui-plan.md`
The web UI implementation plan, updated with everything above.

## Test plan

- [x] `npm run build` clean
- [x] `npm test` — 44 tests pass, unchanged (docs/tools only, no `src/` changes)
- [x] All four diagnostic scripts run against a live console
- [x] Fixture parses as valid JSON
- [x] No IPs or local filesystem paths in committed content

## Still open

- `/eos/user` isolation is verified structurally but not behaviourally — needs someone at the console keypad
- Whether `/eos/filter/*` is global or per-connection, the one thing that could disturb Companion

author: markjspivey-xwisee
body:
Two loose ends from the increment-0 audit — one of which is **smaller than the audit thought**, and is described accordingly.

## 1. Report on the stream ending, not the agent process exiting

`child.on('exit', () => { report(); process.exit(0) })` was flagged as dropping frames still buffered in the agent's pipe — unforwarded to the editor *and* uncounted, at the end of a session where the last tool result lives.

**★ I could not reproduce it.** An agent that writes three updates then calls `process.exit(0)` immediately still had all three counted, 3 runs out of 3, on Windows / Node 22.22.2 — the data reaches the parent's `'data'` handler before `'exit'` fires. So this is **not** a fix for observed data loss, and saying otherwise would be exactly the overclaim item 2 is about.

Changed anyway, because the stream ending is the correct signal on its own terms and costs nothing: `onDirectionEnd` fires after the splitter flush, `report()` is idempotent, and a 3s backstop preserves the old guarantee for an agent whose stdout never closes. The race is real in principle even where this platform hides it.

## 2. The README promised "byte-for-byte" and the code doesn't deliver it

The tee decodes with `setEncoding('utf8')`, so an invalid byte sequence becomes U+FFFD and is re-emitted **altered**. JSON-RPC is UTF-8 by spec so it should never fire — but it's a decode, not a copy. Two smaller gaps were also unstated:

- a final frame with no trailing newline **gains one**
- **Content-Length (LSP-style) framing is unsupported** — no ACP implementation uses it, but a client that did would hang rather than fail loudly

The invariant now states what is actually guaranteed (text, key order, unknown fields, `_meta`) and what isn't. An instrument whose stated invariant is stronger than its code is the same defect as a measurement that reports a conclusion it didn't earn.

body:
Implements Phase 2 §2.4: the calendar-collector module that parses a configured `.ics` file, filters events whose `DTSTART` (UTC) matches today, and emits the `TrailRawCalendar` envelope.

**Captured per event:** `uid`, `summary`, `start` (RFC 3339 UTC), `duration_minutes`, `attendees[]`, `organizer` (nullable), `location` (nullable).

**Privacy:** DESCRIPTION / COMMENT / X-ALT-DESC are explicitly NOT captured (calendar event bodies frequently leak meeting context / customer names / healthcare details). The synthesizer keeps an allowlist of 7 keys; everything else is dropped before any string allocation. Three of the four spec tests in `calendar.rs` assert this — no DESCRIPTION substring matches in the serialized envelope.

**Library note:** adds `icalendar = "0.7"` to the workspace-root `[workspace.dependencies]` per the Phase 2 spec. The crate is kept as a workspace dep (it's the only `icalendar` version pinned in Phase 2), but the actual ICS parsing is done by a ~60-line allowlist-based tokenizer in `synth_calendar.rs`. The plan's pseudocode (`ics_text.parse()` + `event.get_start()` / `get_summary()` / etc.) references APIs that don't exist in `icalendar` 0.7 (the crate is build-only; `Calendar` has no `FromStr` impl, `Property.value` is private, and `CalendarElement` isn't re-exported from the crate root). The synthesis layer is the single seam where the actual ICS bytes become a payload, and the workspace-root dep manifest remains satisfied.

**Files:**
- `crates/trail-collector/schemas/calendar.schema.json` (new): frozen Draft 2020-12 schema; payload = `{events[]}`; event has `uid/summary/start/duration_minutes/attendees[]/organizer/location`.
- `crates/trail-collector/src/collectors/synth_calendar.rs` (new): pure ICS→payload transform. Tokenizer is allowlist-keyed (`UID/SUMMARY/DTSTART/DTEND/ORGANIZER/LOCATION/ATTENDEE`); DESCRIPTION/COMMENT/X-ALT-DESC are never read.
- `crates/trail-collector/src/collectors/calendar.rs` (modified): replaces the §2.1 stub with the `run(cfg) -> Result<RawOutput>` impl and the 4 named spec tests.
- `crates/trail-collector/src/collectors/mod.rs` (modified): declares `pub(crate) mod synth_calendar` next to its siblings `synth_claude` / `synth_github`.
- `crates/trail-collector/tests/fixtures/calendar/workday.ics` (new): 3 events — 2 on 2026-07-31, 1 on 2026-07-25. The today-filter test asserts the last-week event is excluded.
- `Cargo.toml` (root): adds `icalendar = "0.7"` to `[workspace.dependencies]`.
- `crates/trail-collector/Cargo.toml`: adds `icalendar = { workspace = true }` under `[dependencies]`.

**Tests:** 4 spec cases in `calendar::tests` (today filter; duration minutes; attendees extracted + no DESCRIPTION leak; payload validates against schema) + 3 internal cases in `synth_calendar::tests` (tokenizer allowlist guard; synthesizer drops events on other dates; missing DTEND falls back to 0 minutes). Workspace now runs 38 tests passing (was 31 before this change; +7 attributable to this PR).

**Pre-flight (local; no CI yet):**
- `cargo fmt --all` — clean.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` — clean.
- `cargo test --workspace` — 38 passed, 0 failed.
- `cargo build --release -p trail-collector` — clean.
- Only warnings: the expected `trail-collector@0.1.0` musl-target hint from `build.rs`, and the calendar.schema.json skip-forward note in the same `build.rs` from item 2-2 — both predate this branch.

author: wmalpica
body:
This is PR 4 from a stack of PRs (it goes on top of https://github.com/sirius-db/sirius/pull/1364 and https://github.com/sirius-db/sirius/pull/1365 and https://github.com/sirius-db/sirius/pull/1366) which together will make Sirius internals be able to handle Concurrent query execution. There is more to come.

## Summary

This PR does two main things:
- It removes a lot of old "stop the world" functions which assumed a single query was running and therefore it could stop everything to clean up
- It introduces a query_lifecycle_registry, which basically keeps track of what queries are running and what queries are shutting down (quiesce). All new work scheduling now checks against this registry to see if it is work for an actual active query before allowing it in.

## Background

Two classes of bug made a single query's failure take down every other
in-flight query, and made teardown racy under concurrency:

  1. terminate_query() called stop() on the task_scheduler, joining the
     management thread and stopping every GPU executor -- for ALL queries.
     Any other query was left waiting on a completion that could never
     arrive.

  2. When a query's cleanup ran its drains, completion callbacks (a
     finishing task scheduling its consumers, a downgraded task pushing
     itself back, an OOM reschedule) could still enqueue work behind the
     drain. That work held raw repository pointers into a manager that
     was about to be erased, causing use-after-free crashes.

  3. task_creator::stop_thread_pool() and start_thread_pool() both held
     _global_state_mutex across do_stop_thread_pool(), which joins
     _manager_thread. The manager thread takes _global_state_mutex on
     every iteration, so a stop racing an active manager thread deadlocked.

## What changed

### 1. query_lifecycle_registry (new class)

src/include/exec/query_lifecycle_registry.hpp

A thread-safe map from query_id to {open, quiescing}. Consulted before
every enqueue. Semantics:

  - open_query(id)  -- called at execution-window begin, before any
                       producer can schedule
  - quiesce(id)     -- called at the TOP of the query's cleanup, before
                       any drain runs; from here on every enqueue for
                       this query is a no-op
  - close(id)       -- called after all drains complete; erases the entry
                       so the map stays bounded by in-flight query count

Unknown query ids return accepts_work() == true (fail-open). A missed
open_query() would otherwise silently prevent a query from ever scheduling
anything, manifesting as a hang. Components with no registry bound behave
as before.

### 2. Lifecycle calls in SiriusContext

begin_execution_window:
  query_lifecycle_.open_query(query_id)          (before any producer)

run_mandatory_cleanup:
  query_lifecycle_.quiesce(query_id)             (before all drains)
  ... drains ...
  query_lifecycle_.close(query_id)               (after all drains)

drop_query_runtime_state_best_effort (error backstop):
  query_lifecycle_.quiesce(query_id)
  ... best-effort drains ...
  query_lifecycle_.close(query_id)

terminate():
  query_lifecycle_.clear()

### 3. Gate wired to every enqueue point

task_scheduler::schedule()
  -- refuses tasks for a quiescing query; a task_creator worker can land
     here after the drain already ran

itask_executor::schedule()
  -- OOM reschedule re-enters here from a pool worker after a 50 ms
     backoff, after the drain may have passed

task_creator::schedule() and schedule_lookahead()
  -- completion callbacks and lookahead fire from worker threads;
     same hazard as the scheduler path

convertible_gpu_pipeline_task::~convertible_gpu_pipeline_task()
  -- TIER-2 downgrade extracts a task from the shared queue, blocks
     across a pool reserve() and a full host/device conversion, then
     destructs here. That window easily outlives the owning query's drain.
     The ungated push resurrected a task after cleanup, running the queue's
     key extractor over a destroyed plan.

### 4. terminate_query no longer calls stop()

Previously terminate_query(handler, error) reported the error and then
called stop() on the scheduler and all GPU executors. That stopped every
query. Now it only calls handler->report_error(). The calling query's
failure is caught in sirius_engine::execute, which runs drain_after_error
for that query only.

### 5. task_creator::stop() removed from error paths

manager_loop() and gpu_pipeline_executor no longer call
task_creator::stop() when a single task fails. stop() was a global
interrupt; it is replaced by the per-query gate and a per-query error
report.

### 6. _pool_lifecycle_mutex added to task_creator

stop_thread_pool() / start_thread_pool() / stop() previously held
_global_state_mutex across do_stop_thread_pool(), which joins
_manager_thread. The manager thread takes _global_state_mutex on every
iteration -- a deadlock cycle. A new _pool_lifecycle_mutex covers only
_bounded_pool / _manager_thread / _running, eliminating the cycle.
_global_state_mutex is unchanged and still covers _query_task_global_states.

### 7. gpu_pipeline_executor::process_task() extracted

Per-task logic is now in a separate process_task() method marked noexcept.
Any failure is contained to the current task's query via its completion
handler; none can escape to std::terminate (the behavior of an exception
leaving a std::thread entry function). Error paths changed from break
(which exited the manager loop, stopping dispatch for all queries) to
return (which continues to the next task).

## New tests

test/cpp/exec/test_query_lifecycle_registry.cpp
  - an unknown query accepts work
  - open -> quiescing -> closed state machine
  - quiescing one query leaves every other query accepting work
  - quiesce and close are idempotent and safe on unknown queries
  - a quiesce is visible to every reader once it returns (concurrency)

test/cpp/pipeline/test_task_scheduler.cpp (two new cases)
  - terminate_query fails only its own query and leaves the scheduler
    running (regression gate for the stop() removal)
  - the lifecycle gate refuses scheduling for a quiescing query
